text:
Recent work distinguishes plausible association from actionable recommendation. [Feedback-Grounded Policy Discovery (2026)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27789) separates current-demand interpretation from recommendation policies and rejection boundaries; policies are assessed through outcome feedback rather than linguistic plausibility. [Beyond Facts (ACL 2025)](https://aclanthology.org/2025.acl-long.349/) identifies omitted constraints and invented intent as distinct failure modes. Together, these support evaluating specific evidence-backed matches separately from broad topical similarity; neither establishes willingness to choose from interaction history alone.

A proposed diagnostic taxonomy for this setting: specific match, broad association, redundant alternative, explicit incompatibility, explicit rejection, and insufficient evidence. These are proposed operational labels, not an established taxonomy from the papers. Attach every judgment to ranked item IDs and supporting history events or title/description passages. Treat compatibility as unknown unless available evidence establishes the relevant requirement; distinguish simulator-stated willingness from observed behavior. Measure specific-match versus broad-association rank gaps only on evidence-supported pairs, reporting pair counts, evidence coverage, abstention rate, and uncertainty. Keep redundancy descriptive unless feedback explicitly identifies it as unwanted.

Uncertainty deserves separate reporting: [Explainable Uncertainty Attribution for Sequential Recommendation (2024)](https://www.amazon.science/publications/explainable-uncertainty-attribution-for-sequential-recommendation) addresses unreliable recommendations arising from sparse interactions. For the twenty simulator users, report per-user findings and category counts; do not infer population preferences, diversity/conformity traits, or hidden needs. These probes can generate hypotheses for the single BERT4Rec model, while the pinned macro validation HR@10 remains the selection criterion.
